variants.name: M/1895 cavalry carbine
variants.summary: The cavalry carbine of 1895, and with the near-identical M/1897 mountain-artillery and engineer carbine the shortest of the Norwegian Krags. The butt is halved in length and the wood between the receiver and the rear sight is cut away; there is no bayonet lug. The M/1897 differs from it only in where the rear sling swivel is fitted, and the two were issued in one serial series.

variants.name: M/1912 carbine
variants.summary: The short rifle of 1912, adopted after the long M/1894 was judged unwieldy. It is stocked to the muzzle in the manner of a Lee-Enfield, the bayonet lug moves from the barrel to the fore-end, and the rear sight is set back to just ahead of the receiver to lengthen the sight radius. The action is strengthened over the M/1894's at several points. Its nose cap proved weak, which produced the M/1912/16 and M/1912/18 reworks.

variants.name: M/1930 sharpshooter rifle
variants.summary: The last and best of three attempts at a sharpshooter's Krag, after the M/1923 and M/1925. It has a thick barrel, a shorter fore-end than the long rifle, a chequered pistol grip and a fine-tuned trigger; the barrel carries no rear sight at all, only a receiver-mounted aperture with interchangeable front-sight inserts. Pre-war rifles are built on the M/1894 action, the 1950-51 batch on the M/1912.

images.alt: A bolt-action rifle photographed from the right against a pale grey ground, muzzle to the upper right. The stock is plain walnut without a pistol grip; a flat rectangular steel plate on the right of the receiver is the hinged door of the side magazine, and the bolt handle is a straight stem with a round knob. A tangent rear sight sits on the barrel well forward of the receiver, and the barrel is exposed for its last third with two bands.
images.caption: A Norwegian Krag-Jorgensen M/1894 long rifle. The plate ahead of the trigger guard on the right side is the magazine door, which swings down to let five loose rounds be dropped into the horizontal magazine without opening the bolt.

images.alt: Two views of the same short bolt-action rifle, one above the other on a white ground: the left side above with the muzzle to the right, the right side below with the muzzle to the left. The reddish wooden stock runs the whole length of the barrel to a nose cap, and the rear sight sits immediately ahead of the receiver.
images.caption: A Krag-Jorgensen M/1912 carbine from both sides. This is the short rifle variant, not the M/1894 the main figures on this page describe: the stock runs to the muzzle and the rear sight has moved back against the receiver, which lengthens the sight radius.
